quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What should be recorded before attempting to fix an intermittent Windows crash?
option_a: Exact action time error scope and recent changes
option_b: Only a list of installed applications
option_c: The proposed repair and expected downtime
option_d: The most recent successful Windows Update
explanation: Exact symptom timeline scope and change history preserve evidence; installed apps updates and repair planning may follow once the incident is defined.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Why reproduce a symptom when it is safe to do so?
option_a: To prove the user's description is wrong
option_b: To establish a repeatable baseline for testing theories
option_c: To make every available repair in one session
explanation: A repeatable baseline lets the technician compare one controlled test and its result before and after.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: One application crashes for one user while the same application works for other users on that PC. Which scope should be inspected first?
option_a: A systemwide Windows boot fault
option_b: That application's user-specific profile or data
explanation: One-app one-user scope points toward application/user state before systemwide network or hardware action.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: When should a technician escalate instead of continuing experiments?
option_a: When authorization data safety security or hardware safety limits are reached
option_b: Whenever a reboot takes one minute
explanation: Escalation is appropriate when scope authority safety or data risk exceeds the role.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Which THREE Task Manager actions produce useful first evidence for a vague slow-PC complaint?
option_a: Reproduce the affected workload while observing it
option_b: Sort processes by CPU Memory Disk and Network use
option_c: Identify the process owning sustained activity
option_d: End every process with momentary high use
option_e: Disable every startup item without approval
explanation: A repeatable workload resource measurements and the owning process establish evidence; indiscriminate termination or disablement does not.
source_name: Nexus curriculum team (adapted from seed nexus-authored:slow-PC scenario)

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: A PC is slow for five minutes after sign-in and CPU is near 100 percent. What should be inspected?
option_a: Startup apps and the processes consuming CPU
explanation: The timing and CPU evidence point to sign-in workload and owning processes.
source_name: Nexus curriculum team (adapted from seed nexus-authored:slow-PC scenario)

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: A system drive fills again every week after an approved cleanup. What is the best next step?
option_a: Identify the process or data source causing recurring growth
option_b: Schedule increasingly frequent cleanup without investigation
option_c: Compress the whole volume before measuring what grows
option_d: Replace the drive immediately without confirming capacity needs
explanation: Recurring growth indicates an active writer or retention problem; finding the source addresses the cause instead of repeatedly clearing the symptom.
source_name: Nexus curriculum team (adapted from validated seed: Windows Deep Troubleshooting)

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Why is a process using high CPU not automatically the root cause?
option_a: The use may be expected for the workload being reproduced
option_b: Task Manager cannot attribute CPU use to a process
option_c: High CPU always indicates malware rather than workload
option_d: A CPU reading proves whether storage is healthy
explanation: Measurements need timing workload context and a controlled test to distinguish expected work from the cause of the complaint.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What is the best verification after reducing approved startup load?
option_a: Reboot and repeat the measured sign-in/application workflow
explanation: Repeat the same workload and measure whether performance improved.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: A machine shows no vendor logo or POST indicators. Which layer should be investigated before Windows?
option_a: Power delivery and hardware startup
explanation: Windows has not begun if the machine does not reach POST; operating-system and application tools are premature.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Why capture a BSOD stop code?
option_a: It identifies evidence for driver hardware or system investigation
explanation: The stop code and timestamp make later correlation possible.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Windows starts in Safe Mode after a recent display-driver change. What is a reasonable test?
option_a: Roll back the display driver then boot normally
explanation: Safe Mode plus change history supports a controlled driver rollback test.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Repeated forced power-offs during failed boot attempts create what concern?
option_a: Filesystem and user-data damage
explanation: Hard power-offs can corrupt open data and filesystem state.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Unexpected shutdowns occur only during heavy workloads. Which evidence is useful?
option_a: Temperature power and event history
explanation: Load-related shutdowns warrant thermal/power correlation plus Windows records.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Which Windows tool presents a day-by-day stability timeline that correlates application failures and system changes?
option_a: Reliability Monitor
explanation: Reliability Monitor provides a stability history organized over time; the other tools show live processes devices or system inventory.
source_name: Nexus curriculum team (adapted from seed nexus-authored:PDF editor crash ticket)

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: A PDF app exports one page but crashes on one large annotated file. What is the strongest next evidence?
option_a: Find the smallest repeatable file/operation boundary
explanation: Narrowing the repeatable boundary supports app/vendor investigation.
source_name: Nexus curriculum team (adapted from seed nexus-authored:PDF editor crash ticket)

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Event Viewer repeatedly records Event 1000 for a crashing application and names addin.dll as the faulting module. What is the best interpretation?
option_a: The add-in is a strong lead that should be isolated and verified
option_b: The named module proves the Windows kernel is corrupt
option_c: The event proves the user's profile cannot be involved
option_d: The event is irrelevant because only BSOD records matter
explanation: A repeatedly named add-in module is a strong diagnostic lead but still requires a controlled isolation test before declaring root cause.
source_name: Nexus curriculum team (adapted from validated seed: Windows Deep Troubleshooting)

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: Which THREE comparisons can help isolate a repeatable application crash?
option_a: Open a different file in the same app
option_b: Run the same operation under another approved user profile
option_c: Test the same file/operation on a known-good workstation
option_d: Change the workstation's IP address without network evidence
option_e: Replace the PSU before checking whether the failure follows the file
explanation: File user and workstation comparisons reveal whether the failure follows data profile application or device; unrelated changes obscure that boundary.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What proves an application-crash fix?
option_a: The exact original operation completes repeatedly without the error
explanation: Verification repeats the action that failed under comparable conditions.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What belongs in a completed troubleshooting ticket?
option_a: Symptom evidence cause/action and verification
explanation: A useful ticket preserves the reasoning and proof for future support.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What Windows tool can be opened with perfmon /rel to show a failure timeline?
explanation: Reliability Monitor is opened by perfmon /rel.

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What Windows startup mode loads a limited set of drivers and services for diagnosis?
explanation: Safe Mode starts Windows with a limited baseline.
acceptable_answers: ["Safe Mode", "safe mode with networking", "safe mode with command prompt"]

quiz_title: A+ Windows Performance, Startup & Application Troubleshooting — Module Bank
question_text: What built-in Windows tool shows live per-process CPU memory disk and network use?
explanation: Task Manager provides the expected live process/resource view.
